dates.title: Production requirement 1 — exact dates and the ten-year timeline
dates.rule: Every on-screen date and time must match this table; tools/script_audit.py checks them against a real calendar.
rows: Night of Monday 12 → Tuesday 13 September, Year 0 (ends 07:00)
The drawing; "When I have time"; caption sighting 1.
"That night, nobody gets tired." The first night without sleep begins.
10 p.m. couch, 1 a.m. montage, 4 a.m. kitchen; sunrise ≈ 06:35.
Economy goes 24/7. Mum takes the night shift. Schools split into shifts (Leo 16, Mia 9).
Leo turns 18 and joins BLACK 24. Mia (11): "Next week." First tally mark; caption sighting 2.
"I GOT IN!! 🎓 Hill before I go?" → 👍. Mum sees the acceptance photo the same night.
Packing. "She leaves tomorrow." Ticket 14 SEP · 07:00; letter TERM STARTS 15 SEPTEMBER.
Moment zero + 10 years + 5 hours. The train is now this morning, 4 hours away.
Still full night at these times (checked below).
Term starts the day after she travels.
dates.not_shown: No year and no Year 10 weekday is ever shown on screen. On-screen dates: 12 SEP (ch 2 wall calendar); 12 MAY · 3:02 A.M., 13 SEPTEMBER · 8 P.M. and 14 SEPTEMBER · 3 A.M. (ch 7 labels); 12 MAY · 03:02 (phone); TERM STARTS 15 SEPTEMBER and 14 SEP · 07:00 (letter and ticket).
moment_zero: Moment zero = the beginning of the first night without sleep: Tuesday 13 September, Year 0, 22:00 (story city, local time).
The night before: Monday 12 September ≈ 22:30 → Tuesday 13 September 07:00, when Leo's household wakes. Nobody ever falls asleep again.
Moment zero + 10 calendar years = 13 September, Year 10, 22:00 — 3,652 or 3,653 days later, depending on how many 29 Februaries fall in between. The Year-10 night is the night of 13 → 14 September.
14 September, Year 10, 03:00 = moment zero + 10 years + 5 hours — the same hour of the same night as 03:00 on 14 September, Year 0, during the first sleepless night.
'Nobody here has slept… in ten years'
Hook − end of the last sleep = 10 years + 20 hours. True.
Why not the other two definitions

Beginning of the last sleep (Mon 22:30) or end of the last sleep (Tue 07:00): with the hook kept at 03:00 on 13 September, the end of the last sleep was only 9 years, 364 days and 20 hours earlier — 'in ten years' would be 4 hours short.

notebook.title: Production requirement 2 — notebook caption and tally legible on a phone
notebook.rule: Legibility beats quantity. Every sighting is an insert (a close-up cut), never a detail in a wide shot.
notebook.caption_text: WHEN LEO / HAS TIME — two lines, thick marker capitals in a child's hand, clean letterforms (no reversed letters, no joined-up writing)
notebook.zone: inside the content zone, y 200–850; nothing in the subtitle band (y 850–1026); no other text in the insert

tally.ch8_layout: three groups of five (four uprights + one diagonal), stacked as a short column under the caption

notebook.phone_checks: Checked at 960×540 and 640×360 at G5 (style samples) and G6 (preview): the caption must read in under 2 s; the tally must read as 'many times'. Pixel-sample the rendered paper and ink: contrast ≥ 7:1 under the scene's lighting.
other_text: 12 MAY · 03:02 (ch 7 phone date header and time)
cap height ≥ 5 % of frame height (≥ 54 px); held ≥ 2.5 s in a gap in the narration
≥ 54 px and ≥ 43 px; each held ≥ 1.5 s

opening_sync.title: Production requirement 3 — the full playground is on screen for the whole first line
rows: The full playground under the 3:00 clock, already in motion, with sound. No black frame, no fade, no pull-back.
Narration starts: "It's three a.m. — and the playground is full."

The playground shot stays on screen and complete: the camera pushes in 2 % at most; every piece of play equipment stays at least 5 % inside the frame edges; the swings, the slide and the clock sit in the content zone (y 200–850), with only ground in the subtitle band.

The first cut comes when the word "full" ends plus 4 frames — never mid-line. If the generated line runs long, the shot runs long and everything after it moves later. The line is never sped up to fit.
0:03.2. At Video #1's measured speaking rate (≈ 192 words/min), the 8 words plus the dash pause end at ≈ 0:02.95, so the cut lands at ≈ 0:03.1.
The thumbnail shot (Leo's eyes) for 1.0 s, then the 'ten years from now' cuts.
Once your MP3 exists, the end of "full" is measured from the word timings and the cut is set from it.
opening_sync.deviation: Story Lock v4 put the thumbnail cut at 0:02.0, and Production Standard v1.3 §6 says the thumbnail image appears 'within the first 3 s'. Requirement 3 makes both impossible: 8 words cannot be spoken naturally in 1.8 s. The cut therefore moves to the end of the line (planned 0:03.2, measured ≈ 0:03.1). Standard v1.4 rewords the rule accordingly (LL-67).

timeline.reference_year_rule: Any year in which 12 September is a Monday. The audit checks every such year from 2026 to 2060.

chapters.title: The Impossible Question
chapters.music: Hook cue: a low pulse under the playground sound from frame 1; a hit on the cut to Leo's eyes; builds through the premise; cuts to silence for the title hit, then a rewind whoosh.

beats.picture: FRAME 1 (0:00.0) — a wide shot already in motion, no pull-back. A floodlit playground packed with children fills the lower two-thirds: two swings at the top of their arc, a slide, kids running. Behind it, the night city: a navy sky without stars, every window lit. Centred above the skyline, a huge luminous analog clock reads 3:00 (teal and cool white). Night, 3:00 and a full playground all read at phone size from the first frame. The whole playground stays in frame for the entire line (opening-sync spec, requirement 3).
beats.sound: From frame 1, no fade-in: children's laughter, swing chains, a distant school bell, traffic hum. Music: low pulse.

lines.text: It's three a.m. — and the playground is full.
lines.timing: starts 0:00.2; the shot holds until 'full' ends + 4 frames

beats.picture: First cut — THE THUMBNAIL SHOT: an extreme close-up of Leo's (25) wide-open eyes at an office window, the 3:00 clock and the floodlit playground reflected in the glass. Subject inside the centred 9:16 column.
beats.sound: A low hit on the cut; the playground sound drops behind glass.

beats.picture: Fast cuts, about 2 s each: a school with every classroom lit; a gridlocked street under the 3:00 clock; back to the swings.
beats.sound: School bell, car horns; the pulse quickens.

lines.text: The schools are open.
Traffic's jammed.
And nobody here has slept… in ten years.

beats.picture: Today: Earth turning in time-lapse. On the night side, windows go dark in waves across a city and a parent switches off a child's lamp; on the day side, a night-shift nurse pulls blackout blinds at noon and lies down.
beats.sound: The music drops to a soft bed; a clock ticking; the city's hush.

lines.text: Sometime today, almost everyone on Earth will lie down… and sleep.
About a third of your life.
More than twenty years.

beats.picture: Leo (15) in bed in the dark; his eyes snap open. (A hook image, not a story moment.)
beats.sound: A sharp whoosh on the eyes opening; the pulse returns.

lines.text: So what if you never needed to sleep again?
Not tired.
No harm done.
Just… awake.

beats.picture: Glimpses: a sunrise after a sleepless night; the 24-hour city at full speed; a child's notebook flipping through blank pages (never Mia's drawing).
beats.sound: The music builds to the title.

lines.text: This is the first twenty-four hours.
The next ten years.
And why, in this world, a whole generation of kids has never had a single dream.

beats.picture: Title card, then the clock's hands spin backwards into chapter 2.
beats.sound: Title hit; a rewind whoosh as the clock spins back.

onscreen.text: WHAT IF HUMANS NEVER NEEDED SLEEP?

chapters.title: The Biological Breakthrough
chapters.music: Curious science cue (light arpeggio); it thins under the unknowns; a tick-tock motif for the clock; it stops for one beat under 'nobody dreams'.

beats.picture: Monday night. Leo (15) yawning over homework; a wall calendar behind him shows 12 SEP (background detail). Mum leans in at the door, then switches off the hall light. Through the next door, Mia (8) asleep, her notebook under her hand.
beats.sound: Room tone; a yawn; Mum's voice from the doorway; the hall light clicks off.

onscreen.text: MONDAY — THE LAST NIGHT ANYONE SLEEPS

lines.text: Goodnight, you two.
First, what does sleep actually do?

beats.picture: Navy science graphic. Three fast icons rise from a sleeping brain: a film strip replaying Leo's guitar chord (memory); virus icons around a nose (immunity); sugar cubes beside an 'age' dial (metabolism).
beats.sound: Science cue; a soft tick as each icon lands.

lines.text: Studies suggest it helps lock in what you learned.
In one study, people sleeping six hours or less… had about four times the odds of catching a cold.
In another, after six short nights, young men handled blood sugar worse.

beats.picture: Two mouse-lab cards land, stamped YES and NO; a question mark settles over a dreaming brain.
beats.sound: Two stamp thuds; the arpeggio thins.

lines.text: Some of it, nobody fully understands.
What's REM sleep for?
Does sleep really clean the brain?

beats.picture: The brain again, with two devices inside. An HOURGLASS whose sand of tiny dots fills as a day passes; its signal travels to a 'sleepy' dial through small sockets. Caffeine shapes from a coffee cup slip into the sockets: the dial reads low, but the sand keeps falling. A small CLOCK deep in the brain, its hands nudged back into place by light from the eyes.
beats.sound: Sand hiss; soft clicks as the sockets fill; a gentle tick-tock.

lines.text: But two systems decide when you get sleepy.
An hourglass — pressure that builds while you're awake.
Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors.
You feel alert… but the hourglass keeps filling.
And a body clock, reset every day, mainly by light.

beats.picture: The hourglass freezes mid-pour; the clock keeps ticking. The memory, immunity and metabolism icons keep glowing while the eyes stay open.
beats.sound: The sand hiss stops dead; the tick-tock continues alone.

lines.text: A breakthrough would have to stop the hourglass.
And do all of sleep's work while you're awake.
Even the parts we don't understand.
How?
That's the thought experiment.

beats.picture: THE RULE CARD — four lines appear one by one, each with an icon: no yawn; no harm; the clock ticking; a sleeping face with an empty dream bubble. Under line 4, smaller: 'daydreams stay', with an open-eyed face and a thought bubble.
beats.sound: A soft chime per line; the music stops for one beat under 'nobody dreams'.

onscreen.text: 4 · NO DREAMS — a rule we chose

lines.text: In this world, you're never tired.
Going without sleep never hurts.
Your body clock keeps ticking.
And with no sleep… the dreams go too.
Daydreams stay.

chapters.title: The First 24 Hours
chapters.music: Warm amber cue at breakfast; playful percussion for the 1 a.m. montage; near-silence in the 4 a.m. kitchen; a sunrise swell.

beats.picture: Tuesday breakfast. Mia (8) holds up her drawing: two stick figures on a hill under a sky crowded with stars. Leo (15), grabbing toast on his way out, barely looks. Alone, Mia writes underneath in big capitals. INSERT — caption sighting 1 of 3, held ≥ 2.0 s (notebook spec): WHEN LEO / HAS TIME.
beats.sound: Kettle, toast pop, the front door; then a marker squeaking on paper.

onscreen.spec: notebook spec — sighting 1 of 3, no tally yet

lines.text: Look — it's us, on the hill!
Can we go?
Sure.
When I have time.

beats.picture: 10 p.m. The family on the couch, wide awake; the wall clock reads 10:00.
beats.sound: TV murmur, a clock tick; nobody yawns.

lines.text: That night, nobody gets tired.
Not you.
Not Mum.
Not anyone.

beats.picture: THE 1 A.M. MONTAGE — each beat 1–1.5 s in its own colour pocket of the city: a packed 24-hour gym; a game server crashing under record players; Grandma starting a painting; a student opening a language course; a dad and kid building a treehouse by headlamp; a garage band; then one office where a man in a grey suit books 3 a.m. meetings.
beats.sound: Playful percussion builds — gym clank, game chimes, a guitar chord — and stops dead on Mr. Black's pen click.

lines.text: So what do you do with eight extra hours?
By one a.m., the city is training, gaming, painting, studying.
And one man in a grey suit is booking meetings for three a.m.

beats.picture: Mia in bed, eyes open in the dark, her notebook open at a fresh page beside the pillow. No words.
beats.sound: One soft sustained note; the distant city.

beats.picture: 4 a.m., the dark kitchen, lights off; Leo at the window. In a cut-away brain, a thin line runs from the small clock to a tiny gland at the centre, which gives off a soft indigo glow. He switches on the bright ceiling light: the glow thins, never to zero, while the clock keeps ticking. Off again: the glow slowly returns.
beats.sound: Fridge hum; light-switch clicks; a low shimmer for the glow.

lines.text: At night, your body clock still tells a tiny gland in your brain to release melatonin.
Switch on a bright light, and the gland holds back.
You're not tired.
Your body just knows it's night.

beats.picture: Sunrise over the city. Leo on the balcony, wide awake, squinting into the light.
beats.sound: Birdsong; the music swells with the light.

lines.text: Twenty-four hours awake… and you feel fine.
You just got eight hours back.
Almost three thousand hours a year.
And bosses everywhere did the same maths.

chapters.title: The World Economy
chapters.music: Driving, mechanical cue (ticking hi-hats, synth bass); its rhythm slows as the output curve flattens; it drops out for Mum's empty chair.

beats.picture: A world map. On every continent the crowd icons grow by half — two become three (not double: the claim is +50 %).
beats.sound: The economy cue starts.

onscreen.text: waking hours only · assumes ~8 h of sleep · 7–9 h gives +41 % to +60 %

lines.text: Overnight, humanity's waking time grows by about half.
The waking hours of billions of extra people.

beats.picture: Mr. Black's sign reads BLACK & CO.; the '& CO.' slides off and a neon '24' lights up. Warehouses and call centres glow at 3 a.m.
beats.sound: Neon buzzing on; warehouse beeps; phones ringing.

lines.text: Mr. Black's company becomes BLACK 24.
It never closes.
Even today, about one in six US workers doesn't work a regular daytime schedule.
Now the night shift is just… a shift.

beats.picture: Montage, no on-screen text: a bank, a dentist and a delivery at 3 a.m.; a mattress shop and a sleeping-pill display going dark.
beats.sound: Two quick whooshes.

lines.text: Some jobs boom.
Others shrink.

beats.picture: Split cards: winners (a business owner, a customer) and losers (a worker). The RAND card builds while the figure is spoken: the number, what it measured, its source. Then the scale tips: new costs stack on the other side.
beats.sound: A register ping on 'Winners?'; a low tone under the RAND figure; a dull thud on 'Losers?'.

onscreen.text: missed work · lower productivity · earlier deaths

lines.text: Winners?
Companies and customers.
In twenty sixteen, RAND estimated that lack of sleep cost the US economy… up to four hundred and eleven billion dollars a year.
Missed work.
Lower productivity.
Earlier deaths.
Here, that cost could fall.
Though a nonstop world may bring new costs.
Losers?
Workers.
When everyone can work more, your hour might be worth less.

beats.picture: An output curve rises, flattens past 49 hours a week, and ends in a question mark where a tireless worker stands.
beats.sound: The cue's rhythm slows as the curve flattens.

lines.text: But more hours don't always mean more output.
A study of First World War munitions factories found… each hour past about forty-nine a week added less.
Could you stay focused if you never got tired?
Nobody knows.

beats.picture: Mum signs BLACK 24's night-shift contract. Cut to dinner: her chair is empty; Leo and Mia eat without talking.
beats.sound: A pen scratch; the music drops out — room tone and cutlery only.

lines.text: Mum takes BLACK 24's night shift.
It pays more.
Enough to start Mia's university fund.
Her chair at dinner stays empty.

chapters.title: A City That Never Sleeps
chapters.music: Urban pulse; filtered under the grid graphic; it cuts to a hush on the dark-sky side.

beats.picture: Midnight: Mum, BLACK 24 lanyard on, squeezed into a packed train; the platform clock reads 00:00.
beats.sound: Train doors, crowd murmur, the urban pulse.

lines.text: Mum's train to work leaves at midnight.
It's packed.
New York's subway already runs all night.
Now many cities try.

beats.picture: Engineers with head-torches on empty tracks at night; then the same tracks with trains thundering past the crew.
beats.sound: Echoing tunnel, tools clinking; then a train roars through.

onscreen.text: Night Tube: Fridays and Saturdays only

lines.text: But even today, London keeps its all-night Tube to weekends.
Weeknights are for repairs.
So in a city that never stops… when do you fix it?

beats.picture: Montage: a diner at 3 a.m., an operating theatre at 4 a.m., a concert at 5 a.m. — each with a wall clock.
beats.sound: Diner bell; monitor beep; a crowd roar.

lines.text: Dinner at three.
Surgery at four.
Concerts at five.

beats.picture: A school timetable with three sessions. Mia (9) arrives at 8 a.m.; Leo (16) at 9 p.m.
beats.sound: A school bell, twice — morning, then night.

lines.text: Schools split into shifts.
Mia's starts at eight a.m.
Yours… at nine p.m.

beats.picture: Grid graphic: a lighting load line climbs through the night while the solar line sits at zero; batteries, wind, dams and gas plants slide in to fill the gap.
beats.sound: Electrical hum rising; a power-down blip as the solar line flattens.

lines.text: Lighting in homes, offices and streets already takes an estimated eight percent of the world's electricity.
Keep it on all night, and demand climbs.
Just when solar panels produce nothing.

beats.picture: Stars fading out over the city; birds singing under streetlights; turtle hatchlings crawling toward a promenade's lights instead of the sea.
beats.sound: A thin high tone as the stars fade; birdsong at night; waves.

lines.text: Even now, more than four in five people live under light-polluted skies.
Here, the stars fade faster.
Birds sing at the wrong hour.
Turtle hatchlings lose their way to the sea.

beats.picture: Split screen: a megacity's glare beside a small town under a sky full of stars; the town's streetlights dim on a timer.
beats.sound: The urban cue cuts to a hush on the dark side: crickets, wind.

lines.text: But not every place switches on.
Some towns follow Flagstaff, Arizona — the world's first International Dark Sky City.
They keep their nights dark.
On purpose.
Our guess?
Cities adapt in a year.
People take longer.

chapters.title: The Hidden Cost
chapters.music: A warm reprise of the breakfast theme, thinning as the schedules split; sparse piano; near-silence for the signature line.

beats.picture: Warm amber vignettes of Leo's family in the first weeks: a midnight dinner with all three at the table; a 4 a.m. walk together; Mum reading to Mia.
beats.sound: The warm reprise.

lines.text: Do you spend more time with your family?
At first, you do.

beats.picture: A 24-hour clock with three coloured arcs that barely overlap. Then a small inner clock in each family member's silhouette drifts out of step under lights that never switch off.
beats.sound: The reprise thins to one line; three clock ticks slip out of sync.

lines.text: Then the schedules split.
You're all awake twenty-four hours a day… and almost never together.
Nobody says goodnight anymore.
Even your body clocks drift apart.
The lights never go off.

beats.picture: Leo, 18, gets a BLACK 24 lanyard. He's quick and good at it: three screens, a headset, a nod from Mr. Black.
beats.sound: Office hum; a badge beep.

lines.text: At eighteen, you join BLACK 24 too.
Nights.
You're good at it.
You're always available.

beats.picture: Mia (11) at his door, holding the notebook open at the drawing. Leo, on a call, doesn't turn round. INSERT — caption sighting 2 of 3, held ≥ 2.0 s: WHEN LEO / HAS TIME, and her pencil adds the first tally mark beneath.
beats.sound: Call chatter; one pencil stroke, loud in the quiet.

onscreen.text: WHEN LEO / HAS TIME + 1 tally mark

lines.text: Next week.

beats.picture: Leo's night off: 3 a.m., lying on his bed with a book. His phone lights up — MR. BLACK: “You're up, right?” He puts the book down and answers.
beats.sound: Phone buzz; a sigh; a keyboard.

lines.text: Sleep was the one excuse nobody could argue with.
Now nobody's ever asleep.
France and Australia already give workers a right to disconnect.
Work was leaking into our nights long before this.

beats.picture: An inverted-U curve of free time against well-being. Past about five hours it splits: one branch stays level (someone learning the cello; someone caring for a parent), the other dips (someone scrolling at 4 a.m.).
beats.sound: Sparse piano; the tick of a scrolling phone.

lines.text: Would more time make you happier?
Research suggests free time helps… up to about two hours a day.
Past about five, well-being can actually dip.
lines.review: it marks the surprising direction S40 found (more free time, lower well-being); it does not inflate the size

lines.text: Unless that time goes into something productive.
Some people flourish.
Some just drift.

beats.picture: Mia turns the pages: one drawing, then blank page after blank page.
beats.sound: Page turns, nothing else.

lines.text: Mia's notebook stays blank.
And science still hasn't settled what dreams were for.

beats.picture: The signature line on screen, white on near-black, each half appearing as it is spoken.
beats.sound: Near-silence; one low piano note.

onscreen.text: WE DIDN'T LOSE SLEEP. / WE LOST THE NIGHT.

lines.text: We didn't lose sleep.
We lost the night.

chapters.title: Ten Years Later
chapters.music: A wide cinematic cue; it drops to intimate piano at Leo's desk; the clock's ticking returns at 'three a.m.'.

beats.picture: The city at 3 a.m., brighter and denser than in chapter 5.
beats.sound: A wide swell.

lines.text: Imagine it's ten years on.
You're twenty-five.

beats.picture: Earth from orbit; the night side's city lights brighter and wider than in the chapter 1 shot.
beats.sound: A low orbital drone.

lines.text: From space, Earth's night side glows brighter than ever.

beats.picture: The giant 3:00 clock over a jammed street — the hook's composition again.
beats.sound: Rush-hour traffic at full volume.

lines.text: Three a.m. is just another rush hour.
Days don't end anymore… they change shifts.

beats.picture: Trains run nose to tail; small robots repair a tunnel wall between them.
beats.sound: Rail rhythm; servo whirs.

lines.text: Trains never stop.
Robots fix the tunnels between them.

beats.picture: BLACK 24 logos everywhere — on trucks, towers and uniforms.
beats.sound: The cue's bass hits.

lines.text: The economy is bigger.
But for many people, the working week crept up… not down.

beats.picture: A coach of tourists in a dark-sky town, every face turned up to the stars; then a QUIET HOURS sign on a parliament's steps.
beats.sound: Crickets and a hushed crowd; then a gavel.

lines.text: Darkness is a luxury now.
People travel just to see stars.
Some countries pass night laws.
Hours when nobody can be called to work.

beats.picture: A classroom at 3 a.m. A teacher describes dreams like ancient history; a child's hand goes up — a speech bubble on screen, not voiced: “What did it feel like?”
beats.sound: Classroom murmur, then quiet.

lines.text: The biggest change of all?
A whole generation of children… who have never had a single dream.

beats.picture: Label: 12 MAY · 3:02 A.M. Leo at a BLACK 24 control desk. His phone lights up — MESSAGE INSERT, held ≥ 2.5 s in a gap in the narration: date header 12 MAY, time 03:02; MIA: “I GOT IN!! 🎓 Hill before I go?” He sends 👍 without looking up.
beats.sound: Control-room hum; a message chime; one thumb tap.

onscreen.text: MIA: I GOT IN!! 🎓 Hill before I go?

lines.text: And you?
You run night operations at BLACK 24.

beats.picture: Later that same night: Mum in the warehouse, older, still on nights. On her phone, a photo of Mia's acceptance letter; she smiles.
beats.sound: Warehouse hum; the piano.

lines.text: Mum's nights paid for Mia's place at university.

beats.picture: Label: 13 SEPTEMBER · 8 P.M. Mia (18) packing. The letter on her bed: NEUROSCIENCE · TERM STARTS 15 SEPTEMBER. Her ticket: 14 SEP · 07:00. The notebook goes into her bag last.
beats.sound: A zip; tape; a quiet piano phrase.

lines.text: She leaves tomorrow.
To study the brain… and find out what dreams were for.

beats.picture: Label: 14 SEPTEMBER · 3 A.M. — midnight has passed, so her train is now this morning. The skyline clock's minute hand reaches 12: 3:00. Match cut to the office window from the hook.
beats.sound: The ticking returns, then stops on the hour.

lines.text: Which brings us back to three a.m.

chapters.title: The Final Question
chapters.music: A quiet pad in the office; music only for the run; the stars cue swells gently; 1.5 s of silence before the reality line; the last line resolves into silence before the mark. No outro.

beats.picture: 3:00 a.m. — the hook's shot, now understood: Leo at his desk by the office window, the playground below.
beats.sound: The playground behind glass, as in 1.2.

lines.text: You're at your desk, like every night.

beats.picture: Mia (18) arrives at his desk from the glass lobby, backpack on, holding the old notebook.
beats.sound: Lobby doors; office hum; the music very low.

lines.text: My train's at seven.
Come to the hill with me.
Just tonight.
I can't.
I'm on shift.

beats.picture: She sets the notebook on his desk and goes. He flips it open — blank pages — then back, back, to the last drawing. INSERT — caption sighting 3 of 3, held ≥ 2.0 s: WHEN LEO / HAS TIME above three groups of five tally marks. He looks up at the analog skyline clock: just past three (the minute hand two minutes past 12).
beats.sound: Footsteps going; page flips; silence on the insert.

onscreen.text: WHEN LEO / HAS TIME + 15 tally marks (3 × 5)

lines.text: When Leo has time.

beats.picture: He stands and grabs the notebook; his chair spins empty — an echo of Mum's chair. He runs.
beats.sound: Music only: the run cue begins; a chair creak.

beats.picture: Leo's car leaves the glow. His phone lights up — MR. BLACK: “Where are you?” — and he switches it off. Past the last streetlight, stars appear.
beats.sound: Engine; a buzz cut short; the city noise falls away.

lines.text: Out past the last streetlight, the stars come back.

beats.picture: The hill. Mia holds the drawing up against the real sky: the same hill, the same stars. No words.
beats.sound: Wind in the grass; the stars cue swells.

beats.picture: They lie in the grass, awake, under a sky crowded with stars; the city is only a faint glow on the horizon behind them. No science graphic — just the dark.
beats.sound: Crickets; the music holds one chord.

lines.text: Up here, the lights are finally off.
It isn't sleep.
It's just night.

beats.picture: Mia, eyes closed, a half-smile. Leo smiles.
beats.sound: Crickets.

lines.text: Don't fall asleep on me.
Goodnight, Mia.

beats.picture: 1.5 s of stillness; then the camera rises from the two of them into the stars.
beats.sound: 1.5 s of silence, then a soft pad.

lines.text: Back in the real world, experts recommend adults get at least seven hours a night.
Sleep helps memory, immunity, metabolism… and more we're still learning about.

beats.picture: Hold on the stars.
beats.sound: The music resolves into silence under the last words.

lines.text: If you never had to sleep again… what would you do with the life you got back?

beats.picture: The EXIT CODE mark. No outro.
beats.sound: Silence, then the mark's sound.

fact_bank_notes.G05: Listed in the Lock v4 FACT BANK by mistake: it hasn't been narrated since v3 (it now only grounds SP-10). Errata added to the Story Lock.
fact_bank_notes.B02: Still not narrated: the build-up claim (adenosine as one of the signals behind sleep pressure) would need a hedge and more time. Caffeine's effect is now explained with B03 alone: 'Coffee blocks a sleep signal called adenosine. The hourglass keeps filling anyway.'
fact_bank_notes.B07: No longer used: 'your body's signal of night' was cut from chapter 3 in v4 (the line now says how the clock times melatonin).
fact_bank_notes.B08: Not narrated; governs the chapter 3 picture (the glow thins, never to zero) and the partial verb 'fades'.
fact_bank_notes.HR6: Background rule, shown rather than said: Mia lying in bed (3.4); lying on the hill (8.7).
fact_bank_notes.SP-16: Optional; not used (Lock decision 4 — no room).
fact_bank_notes.B04: Shown, not said: the picture draws the master clock deep in the brain; the narration says 'a body clock'.
fact_bank_notes.B06: Narrated in chapter 3 only, on the first sleepless night when every clock is still normal, as 'At night… releases melatonin' (clock-driven; light suppresses it).
fact_bank_notes.B05: Narrated in chapter 2 ('reset every day, mainly by light'). No longer used in chapter 8, which now makes no circadian claim about Leo.

changes.from: At night, a tiny gland in your brain still releases melatonin. / Your body's signal of night.
changes.to: At night, your body clock still tells a tiny gland in your brain to release melatonin.
changes.why: Names who sets the timing: the body clock drives the pineal gland's nightly release (B06). The old line left the timing unexplained. 'Your body's signal of night' is cut — the beat's last line ('Your body just knows it's night') already says what melatonin means.

changes.from: Switch on a bright light, and it fades.
changes.to: Switch on a bright light, and the gland holds back.
changes.why: Light suppression is a second, separate effect: light holds back the release the clock has timed. It doesn't reset the clock, and it doesn't drain melatonin away. 'Fades' blurred the two. The picture now shows a line from the clock to the gland, the glow thinning under the light while the clock keeps ticking, and the glow returning when the light goes off.

changes.from: Your body clock just knows it's night.
changes.to: Your body just knows it's night.
changes.why: The beat's first line now says 'your body clock', so the last line goes back to the shorter v1 wording.

changes.from: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, so the hourglass feels emptier than it is.
changes.to: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors. / You feel alert… but the hourglass keeps filling.
changes.why: An hourglass can't 'feel', and 'emptier' made listeners work out which way the sand runs. The new pair says the mechanism (receptors blocked), the effect (you feel alert — B03) and the limit (the pressure keeps building) in plain words, still 12 words, and links straight to 2.5's 'stop the hourglass'.

changes.from: Tonight, almost everyone on Earth will lie down in the dark and sleep.
changes.to: Sometime today, almost everyone on Earth will lie down… and sleep.
changes.why: 'Tonight… in the dark' implied one shared night-time schedule; people sleep at different hours, and many by day. 'Sometime today' keeps the sweep and the immediacy of the opening, and what it claims is true: almost everyone sleeps within the day. The picture adds a night-shift nurse pulling blackout blinds at noon, inside the same montage beat. Two words shorter.

changes.from: Cities adapted in a year. / People took longer.
changes.to: Our guess? / Cities adapt in a year. / People take longer.
changes.why: 'Cities adapted in a year' sounded like a forecast, or like history. It is a speculative scenario (SP-05), and 'Our guess?' says so in two words — our ledger defines that class as 'our reasoned guesses'. The present tense matches the chapter. The bridge into chapter 6 is unchanged.
